prompt: State the CAP theorem precisely. During a network partition, what is the real choice?

src.ref: Ch.9 — Linearizability and the cost of the CAP theorem

reveal:
Gist: when the network splits a cluster in two — a **partition**, where some machines can't reach others — a data store must pick one of two things to keep: staying **consistent** or staying **available**. It can't have both while partitioned.

The three properties, spelled out: **Consistency** — every read sees the latest write; **Availability** — every request gets a non-error response; **Partition tolerance** — the system keeps working even when the network drops messages between nodes. CAP says you can't guarantee all three at once.

Since partitions are a fact of life you can't opt out of, the real choice *during* one is C vs A: refuse some requests to stay consistent (a **CP** system), or serve possibly-stale data to stay available (an **AP** system). **Tell:** CAP really means 'pick C or A when partitioned' — not the folk version 'pick any 2 of 3.'

see.label: Brewer — CAP Twelve Years Later: How the Rules Have Changed

prompt: Why is idempotency critical in distributed systems, and give one way to make a non-idempotent operation safe to retry.
reveal:
Gist: an **idempotent** operation gives the same result whether you apply it once or ten times — so it's safe to retry. That matters because networks drop and duplicate messages, forcing clients to retry, and retrying a *non*-idempotent op (like 'add $100') can double-apply and corrupt state.

Make a non-idempotent op safe with an **idempotency key**: the client attaches a unique id to the request, the server records it, and on seeing a duplicate key it returns the stored prior result instead of running the operation again. **Tell:** 'must be safe to retry' = make it idempotent, usually with a dedup key.

prompt: What problem does a consensus algorithm (Raft/Paxos) solve, and why is a majority quorum the key mechanism? What happens with an even split?
reveal:
Gist: a **consensus** algorithm gets a group of machines to agree on one value — or on one ordering of a log of commands — even when some of them crash or messages get lost. That agreement is what lets a cluster of many machines behave like a single, reliable one.

What it's used for: electing a **leader**, and keeping a **replicated log** — every node applies the same commands in the same order, so they all end up in the same state (a 'replicated state machine'). **Raft** and **Paxos** are the two canonical algorithms.

The key mechanism is a **majority quorum** — more than half the nodes (N/2+1) must agree before anything counts. Why a majority specifically: any two majorities must **overlap in at least one node**. So when a new leader is elected by some majority, that majority is guaranteed to include a node that saw the most recent committed entry — which stops two different histories from diverging.

**The even-split case:** if a partition cuts the cluster so no side holds a majority, *neither* side can make progress — the system stalls. That's deliberate: stalling is safer than letting two halves each elect a leader and accept conflicting writes. It's also why clusters use an **odd** number of nodes — an odd count can't split into two equal halves, so one side always keeps a majority.

see.label: Raft paper — In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Ongaro & Ousterhout)
The Secret Lives of Data — Raft visualized

prompt: Contrast synchronous vs asynchronous replication. What does each cost, and how does it relate to the durability/latency tradeoff?
reveal:
Gist: **replication** keeps copies of your data on multiple machines. The single question that defines the tradeoff: does the primary wait for the copies to confirm a write before it tells the client 'done'?

**Synchronous replication:** the primary waits for the replicas to acknowledge the write before confirming to the client. You get strong **durability** (the write survives a crash — it's already on multiple machines) and consistency, but every write pays the latency of the *slowest* replica, and a single slow or dead replica can stall writes entirely.

**Asynchronous replication:** the primary confirms to the client immediately, then streams the change to replicas afterward. Fast and available, but if the primary crashes before the change reaches the replicas, that not-yet-copied tail of writes is **lost** — weaker durability, and reads from a lagging replica can be stale.

This is the **durability-vs-latency tradeoff** in one knob. Many systems split the difference with **semi-synchronous** replication: wait for just *one* replica to acknowledge, not all of them.

prompt: You must shard a stream of keyed events across N servers so the same key always lands on the same server, and adding a server shouldn’t reshuffle everything. What technique, and why not plain hash-mod-N?

src.ref: Ch.6 — Partitioning by hash of key (consistent hashing)

reveal:
Gist: to keep the same key always landing on the same server *and* avoid reshuffling everything when you add a server, use **consistent hashing** — a hash ring — instead of plain hash-mod-N.

Why not plain `hash(key) % N`: the `% N` ties every key's destination to the server count N. Change N — add or remove one server — and the remainder changes for **nearly every key**, so almost all keys move at once. In a cache that means mass invalidation and a stampede to the database.

**Consistent hashing** instead places both servers and keys on a ring (picture positions around a clock face). A key belongs to the next server **clockwise** from it. Now add or remove a server and you only disturb the keys in that one server's arc of the ring — the rest don't move. So only about **K/N keys move** (K keys spread over N servers), not all K.

One refinement: **virtual nodes** — give each physical server many scattered positions around the ring instead of one. That smooths the distribution so no single server gets a lopsided arc.

prompt: Why can’t you trust wall-clock timestamps to order events across machines? What do logical/vector clocks give you instead?
reveal:
Gist: you can't trust wall-clock timestamps to order events across machines, because each machine's clock **drifts** and they're never perfectly in sync. A smaller timestamp on machine A doesn't reliably mean its event happened before one on machine B — you can even get orderings that are physically impossible.

The fix is a **logical clock** — a counter that tracks *causality* (what caused what) instead of physical time. **Lamport clocks** give each event a counter with one guarantee: if event A caused event B, then `clock(A) < clock(B)`. That yields a consistent ordering for events that are causally related.

But Lamport clocks have a blind spot: a smaller counter doesn't *prove* one event caused another, so they can't tell you whether two events are truly independent. **Vector clocks** fix that. Instead of one counter, each node keeps a vector of counters — one slot per node — so you can **detect concurrency**: given two events, tell whether they're causally ordered or genuinely independent (happened with no influence between them). That's the thing plain logical clocks can't do.

see.label: Lamport — Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System

prompt: Name the fallacies of distributed computing that bite most often, and what each implies for your design.
reveal: The **fallacies of distributed computing** are eight false assumptions engineers make about networks. The ones that bite most: *the network is reliable* (so every call needs timeouts and retries), *latency is zero* (so chattiness kills you — batch your calls), *bandwidth is infinite* (payload size matters), *the network is secure* (authenticate and encrypt even internally), and *topology never changes* (use service discovery, not hardcoded hosts). The remaining three: *there is one administrator*, *transport cost is zero*, and *the network is homogeneous*. **The unifying lesson:** in a distributed system, **partial failure** — some parts working while others fail — is the normal case, and every remote call can fail, hang, or succeed while *appearing* to fail.

prompt: A request times out. What do you actually know, and what does that imply for retries?
reveal:
Gist: when a request times out, you've learned almost **nothing** about what actually happened — and that ambiguity is the core difficulty of distributed systems.

A timeout is consistent with four different realities: the request never arrived; it arrived and is still executing; it completed but the **response** was lost on the way back; or the remote node is simply dead. From the caller's side these are indistinguishable — in particular you **cannot tell a slow node from a dead one**.

The big implication is for **retries**. Because the operation might have already run, a blind retry can double-apply it — so retries demand **idempotency**: give the request a unique **idempotency key** the server deduplicates on, so a repeat is harmless.

Two more retry disciplines: use **exponential backoff with jitter** — wait longer after each failure, plus a random offset — so that many clients retrying at once don't synchronize into a **retry storm** that hammers the server in lockstep. And put a **cap or circuit breaker** on retries, so you stop hammering a struggling service instead of finishing it off with load from its own clients.

prompt: Explain two-phase commit and its fundamental weakness. What is the practical alternative?

src.ref: Ch.9 — Atomic commit and two-phase commit (2PC)

reveal:
Gist: **two-phase commit (2PC)** makes several separate databases commit a transaction all-or-nothing, coordinated by one node. Its fatal flaw is that a crash of that coordinator can freeze everyone.

**The two phases.** A **coordinator** runs the show. Phase 1 — **prepare**: it asks every participant 'can you commit this?' Each participant durably promises it *can* — writing the change to disk and **locking** the affected resources — and votes yes or no. Phase 2 — **commit/abort**: if every vote was yes, the coordinator tells all participants to COMMIT; if any said no, it tells them all to ABORT.

**The fundamental weakness: it's a blocking protocol.** If the coordinator crashes *after* participants have prepared but *before* it sends the decision, those participants are stuck — they've locked resources and promised to commit, but they can't decide on their own whether to finish or roll back. They hold the locks indefinitely, waiting. The coordinator is a **single point of failure** that can freeze the whole system.

**Practical alternatives:** the **saga** pattern — break the distributed transaction into a sequence of *local* transactions, each with a **compensating action** that undoes it if a later step fails. Or make the operation **idempotent** and go **eventually consistent**, using an **outbox** (record intended messages in the same local transaction) plus retries.

prompt: Define eventual consistency and read-your-writes consistency. Why does the weaker model surprise users?

src.ref: Ch.5 — Problems with replication lag: reading your own writes

reveal:
Gist: **eventual consistency** promises only that if writes stop, all copies will *eventually* agree — with no bound on *when*, and stale reads allowed in the meantime. **Read-your-writes** consistency adds one guarantee on top: a user always sees their *own* updates, even if they can't yet see other people's.

Why the weaker model surprises users — the classic scenario: you post a comment, the page reloads, and the reload happens to hit a **replica that's lagging** behind and hasn't received your write yet. Your comment is gone. To you that reads as a **bug**, even though the system is behaving exactly as specified — 'eventually' just hadn't arrived.

**Fixes** that buy read-your-writes: route a user's reads to the *same* replica that accepted their write, or read from the **leader** (the authoritative copy) for a short window right after they write.

prompt: What does leader election give you, and what is a split brain? How is it prevented?

src.ref: Ch.8 — The truth is defined by the majority (fencing tokens)

reveal:
Gist: electing a single **leader** gives you one place where all writes are ordered, so there's never a conflict about what happened first. The danger is **split brain** — two nodes both thinking they're the leader.

What a leader buys you: it's a **serialization point**. Every write goes through one node, so the order of writes is unambiguous and you sidestep write-write conflicts entirely.

**Split brain** is the failure: a network partition separates the nodes, and each side elects (or keeps) its *own* leader, so now **two leaders** are both accepting writes. The result is divergent state that may be impossible to reconcile later.

**Prevention, two layers.** First, require a **majority quorum** to elect a leader: since any two majorities overlap in at least one node, only *one* side of a partition can gather a majority — the minority side can't crown a rival. Second, **fencing tokens**: hand each leader a **monotonically increasing epoch number**, and have the storage layer reject any write carrying an old token. So even if a stale leader lingers and tries to write, its outdated token gets it turned away.

prompt: How do failure detectors work, and what is the fundamental tradeoff in choosing a timeout?
reveal:
Gist: a **failure detector** decides a node is dead when its **heartbeats** — periodic 'I'm alive' pings — stop arriving within a **timeout**. The whole game is choosing that timeout, and there's no free choice.

**The tradeoff.** A **short** timeout detects real failures fast — but under a burst of transient slowness it produces **false positives**, declaring a healthy-but-overloaded node dead. That triggers an unnecessary **failover**, which itself adds load and can **cascade** into more false deaths. A **long** timeout avoids the false positives but leaves requests hanging on a node that is genuinely dead. Since you fundamentally **can't distinguish slow from dead**, every timeout is a bet.

**Better than a binary verdict:** a **phi-accrual** failure detector. Instead of a yes/no 'dead,' it watches the *distribution* of recent heartbeat arrival times and outputs a continuous **suspicion level** — how anomalous the current silence is — letting each caller pick its own threshold for acting.

prompt: What are the strategies for partitioning data, and what is a hot spot?

src.ref: Ch.6 — Skewed workloads and relieving hot spots

reveal:
Gist: **partitioning** (sharding) splits data across machines, and you pick between two schemes that trade **range-scan speed** against **even spread**.

**Range partitioning** keeps keys **sorted** across partitions, so range scans ('everything from Monday to Friday') are efficient. The catch: sequential keys like timestamps all fall in the same range, so every write piles onto **one** partition.

**Hash partitioning** runs each key through a hash first, spreading writes **evenly** — but it scatters neighboring keys everywhere, so it **destroys range-scan locality**.

A **hot spot** is a partition getting disproportionate traffic — a celebrity user everyone reads, a trending item, or a monotonic key funneling all writes to one place. **Mitigations:** add a random or hashed **prefix** to a hot key to spread it across partitions (cost: reads must now gather from all of them); use **consistent hashing with virtual nodes** for even distribution; or **split** a hot partition into smaller ones dynamically.

prompt: Contrast B-trees and LSM-trees. Which write pattern favors each, and what is write amplification?
reveal:
Gist: **B-trees** and **LSM-trees** are the two storage-engine designs behind most databases. B-trees favor reads and update data **in place**; LSM-trees favor writes and only ever append.

**B-trees** update pages **in place** — to change a value, you overwrite the page holding it. Reads are fast and predictable (a handful of page lookups down the tree), but writes cause **random I/O** across the disk, and even a tiny change may force rewriting a whole page. Good for read-heavy, update-in-place workloads.

**LSM-trees** (log-structured merge-trees) instead **buffer writes in memory**, then flush them to disk **sequentially** as **immutable sorted files**, never overwriting. A background process **compacts** those files — merging them and discarding superseded values. Sequential writes give excellent **write throughput**, but a read may have to check **several levels** of files (softened by **bloom filters** — a compact probabilistic index that quickly says 'this file definitely does not have your key'), and compaction eats background I/O.

**Write amplification** is the ratio of bytes actually written to disk to the bytes the application asked to write. **Both** designs amplify — B-trees by rewriting pages, LSM-trees by rewriting data during compaction — and it's the key metric for **SSD lifetime** and sustained throughput, since flash wears out with each write.

prompt: What is backpressure and what happens in a system that lacks it?
reveal:
Gist: **backpressure** is a slow consumer telling the upstream producer 'slow down, I can't keep up.' Without it, a fast producer overwhelms a slow consumer and the system falls apart.

What goes wrong with no backpressure: the producer fills queues **without bound**. Memory grows until the process is **OOM-killed** (the OS kills it for exhausting memory). Latency climbs as queues deepen — called **bufferbloat** — and by the time an item is finally dequeued it may already be **stale or irrelevant**.

**Mechanisms that provide it:** **bounded queues** that **block** the producer when full; **credit-based flow control**, where the consumer hands out 'credits' for how much it can accept (TCP does exactly this with its **receive window**); **load shedding** — drop or reject requests early with a clear error rather than queue them; and **rate limiting**. **The design rule:** every queue must be **bounded**, and you must decide **explicitly** what happens when it fills — block, drop, or reject.

prompt: Is exactly-once delivery possible? Explain the distinction people usually mean.
reveal:
Gist: exactly-once **delivery** is impossible — but exactly-once **processing** is achievable, and that distinction is the whole answer.

**Why delivery can't be exactly-once:** over an unreliable network the sender can never be *certain* its message arrived (the acknowledgment itself can be lost). So it must choose between two risks: give up after one try and risk **loss** (**at-most-once**), or keep retrying and risk **duplication** (**at-least-once**). There's no third option that guarantees precisely one delivery.

**What systems actually deliver is exactly-once *processing*** (also called effectively-once): use **at-least-once** delivery, then add **deduplication** or **idempotent** operations so that duplicates have **no observable effect**. The message may arrive twice; it only *counts* once.

**How it's implemented:** attach a unique **message id** and keep a durable **dedup log** to reject repeats; or make the state update **atomic with the offset commit** — Kafka's transactional writes tie 'I processed this' and 'I recorded my position' into one indivisible step. **The mantra:** you can't prevent duplicates — you can only make them harmless.

prompt: Compare cache-aside, write-through, and write-behind. What is a cache stampede and how do you stop it?

src.ref: Ch.11 — Databases and streams (caches as derived data; strategies via secondary reference)

reveal:
Gist: three caching strategies differ in **when the database gets written** relative to the cache; a **cache stampede** is a swarm of requests all missing the same key at once.

**Cache-aside** (lazy loading): the app checks the cache first, and on a **miss** loads from the database and populates the cache itself. Simplest and most common — but data can go **stale**, and every miss pays the cost of a full load.

**Write-through:** every write goes to the cache **and** the database together, synchronously. The cache stays consistent with the database — at the cost of extra **write latency**.

**Write-behind** (write-back): write to the cache and flush to the database **asynchronously** later. Fastest writes, but a crash before the flush **loses data**.

**A cache stampede** (thundering herd): a popular key expires, and many concurrent requests all miss simultaneously and **hammer the database at once** to recompute it. **Stops:** a **lock / single-flight** so only *one* request recomputes while the rest wait; **probabilistic early expiration** — let requests refresh slightly before expiry, staggered, so they don't sync up; or serve the **stale** value while refreshing in the background.

see.label: AWS — Database Caching Strategies (cache-aside, write-through, write-behind)

prompt: What does splitting a monolith into services actually cost? Name the failure modes you inherit.

src.ref: Ch.4 — Dataflow through services: REST and RPC

reveal:
Gist: splitting a **monolith** (one process) into **services** (many networked processes) swaps cheap, reliable in-process function calls for expensive, unreliable network calls — and hands you a pile of new failure modes for the privilege.

**The core trade:** an in-process function call is nanoseconds, always arrives, and can share a transaction. A network call between services is milliseconds, can **fail or hang**, and has **no shared transaction**.

**Failure modes you inherit:** **partial failure** — one service down while others run (the normal case now); **cascading failure** — one slow service saturates its callers' **thread pools**, and the stall spreads upstream; **distributed transactions** — you can no longer commit across services with one simple commit; **versioning and schema compatibility** — services deploy independently, so their message formats drift and must stay compatible; and **debugging** that now needs **distributed tracing**, since a single request crosses many services.

**The real payoff is organizational:** teams deploy and scale their service **independently**. If your org doesn't actually need that independence, the distribution is **pure cost** — you took on all the failure modes and got nothing back.

prompt: When would you choose message queues over direct RPC between services?
reveal:
Gist: choose a **message queue** over direct **RPC** (a remote procedure call — calling another service like a local function and waiting for its answer) when the caller doesn't need an immediate reply and you want the infrastructure to absorb shocks.

**Reach for a queue when:** the caller **doesn't need an immediate answer** to continue; you want to **decouple availability** — the consumer can be down and work simply **buffers** until it returns; you need to **absorb bursts** by smoothing load over time; **multiple consumers** should each see the same event (**fan-out**); or you want **retries** and **dead-lettering** (parking messages that keep failing) handled by the infrastructure rather than your code.

**Stick with direct RPC when:** you need a **synchronous answer** to keep going, the **latency budget is tight**, and the interaction is genuinely request/response.

**The cost of queues:** you buy **eventual consistency**, **ordering** complexity (messages can arrive out of order), and **duplicate delivery** you must handle — usually by making the consumer idempotent.

prompt: How does distributed tracing work, and why are logs alone insufficient?
reveal:
Gist: **distributed tracing** stitches one user request back together as it fans out across many services, so you can see **where the time went**. Logs alone can't do this.

**How it works:** a **trace id** is generated at the **edge** (where the request first enters) and **propagated** through every downstream call via **headers**. Each service emits **spans** — a span records one unit of work with its **start** and **end** time, its **parent span's id**, and metadata — all tagged with the shared trace id. A **collector** gathers the spans and reassembles them into a **causal tree**: the whole request's path, showing which call triggered which and how long each took.

**Why logs alone fall short:** a single request touches many services, each writing to its **own** log with its **own** clock. There's no way to reconstruct which scattered log lines belong to the **same** request, or where the latency actually accumulated.

**The three pillars, each answering a different question:** **tracing** answers 'which hop was slow?'; **metrics** answer 'how often?'; **logs** answer 'what exactly happened?'
